an3.32:1.1: Ānanda (and others) ask a series of similar questions later in the Aṅguttara ([an10.6:1.2](), [an11.7:2.1](), [an11.8:2.1](), [an11.18:2.1]()). See also the next Sutta. | The question is whether it is possible to realize a state of meditative immersion that is based, not just on the temporary suspension of the five hindrances like the regular four absorptions, but on the permanent eradication of all defilements by the arahant. The commentaries identify this state as the “attainment of the fruition of arahantship”.
an3.32:2.1: “I-making” (_ahaṅkāra_) is the ongoing creation of the self or ego through thoughts that reinforce the self. This is most obvious when thinking thoughts in first person. | “Mine-making” (_mamaṅkāra_) is the same, but in regards to things felt to belong to the self, such as one’s body, property, or reputation. | “Underlying tendency to conceit” (_mānānusaya_) is the propensity or compulsion to form a self that remains even when there is no active ego-formation.
an3.32:5.1: This verse is at [snp5.4:6.1]() and is also quoted by the Buddha at [an4.41:6.1](). In both these cases, the verse refers simply to the arahant, not specifically to a special state of meditation. | “The Way to the Far Shore” is the name of the final chapter of the Suttanipāta, especially the sets of questions asked of the Buddha by sixteen brahmins, one of whom was Puṇṇaka. These were contemplative brahmins from a school that identified the cosmic divinity with the state of purified formless consciousness experienced in deep meditation. The title is given in the text itself ([snp5.18:8.4](), [snp5.19:1.1]()), and it is cited also in [sn12.31](), [an3.33](), [an4.41](), [an7.53](), and [an6.61]().
